messages.subject: Distance sampling workshops, August/September 2011,
messages.subject_clean: Distance sampling workshops, August/September 2011,
messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
(CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2011 in our
purpose-built facilities at the University of St Andrews, Scotland. The
aim of these workshops is to train participants in the latest methods
for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and
point transects. The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the
field, using industry-standard software.

The first workshop (30 August - 2 September) will run at an introductory
level, and will focus on "conventional" distance sampling methods, as
described in the standard reference book "Introduction to Distance
Sampling." The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and
participants will learn how to use the program "Distance." Participants
will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of
analysis for distance sampling surveys.  Note this year we have moved
the 'automated survey design' topic out of the advanced workshop into
the introductory workshop.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (5-7 September) will include
advanced treatment of: incorporating covariates in detection function
modelling, analyses in which detectability on the transect line is not
assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and spatial (or
density surface) modelling. The aim of this workshop is to bring
participants up to date with the latest developments in distance
sampling methods and software. It is also an opportunity for those
actively engaged in the design, analysis and execution of distance
sampling surveys to discuss common issues and problems, and set future
research directions. The workshop will be a combination of lectures and
computer sessions, with considerable time for discussion.

For both workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data
sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.
Computer sessions take place in our modern computer classroom (attached
to the seminar room); participants can use our computers or bring their
own laptops.

Additional details regarding the workshop can be found at our website
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/distance2011/workshop_overview.html

strongly from those obtained by bootstrapping:

I know that constraints on the detection function have an influence on =
the
reliability of the analytic estimates of var(h(0)) (Buckland et al. =

=20

ln(s_i) and
regressed g(y_i) on ln(s_i) as proposed by Buckland et al. (2001:75), =
but

=20

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tim, list,

By constraints I guess you mean monotonicity constraints.  Looks like=20
removing those and running the bootstrap results in broadly similar=20
estimate of h(0) - the original (presumably with monotonicity=20
constraint) was 0.62E-2 and the mean of the bootstrapped (presumably=20
without monotonicity constraints) was 0.67E-2.  So, you're getting a big=20
change in estimated variance with little change in estimated h(0).  I=20
rather doubt it's the monotonicity constraint that's making such a large=20
difference - but I don't have any real basis for that statement.  I=20
assume everything else about the model is the same (e.g., it's just one=20
key function and adjustment series in the bootstrap)?  I wonder if you=20
get the same result if you fix the number of series adjustments, as I=20
guess you're allowing them to be selected in each bootstrap rep.  What's=20
the sample size I wonder?  It would also be helpful if you could somehow=20
provide a histogram of the data and the fitted detection function --=20
perhaps you could put that on a web site, or just post the distances if=20
there are not too many?

 From what you've found with the variation in cluster size -- that it=20
has different variance in the bootstrap vs analytic when you estimate=20
variance using the cluster size regression, and similar when you just=20
use mean cluster size -- it seems clear that this is related to the=20
detection function issue above, so we'll need to clear that up first.

Cheers - Len

wrong.  However, your data are unusually long-tailed.  I would be=20
inclined to truncate at say 20m or perhaps 25m, and see if the problem=20
persists.  The hazard-rate model can produce some funny fits, especially=20
for point transect data, and especially when there are relatively large=20
numbers of detections close to the point.  With greater truncation, you=20
may find that e.g. a half-normal model will fit well, and give more=20
stable results.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: Bug in DISTANCE 6.0: Estimation of encounter rate variance
messages.body_plain:
List,

Further to Tim Ritter's report of a problem with CDS point transect variance
estimation, we have confirmed that this is a Bug with the R2 estimator, have
fixed it, and will be issuing a new release of Distance shortly.

The bug report is here:
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=92
More details (from the bug report response) is given below.

  - Len Thomas

From
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=92

The problem was that for estimator P2, a routine was returning the variance of
the estimated encounter rate, when it should have been the standard error --
i.e., a square root was not being taken.

Typically the standard error on encounter rate will be less than 1, and hence
the variance is smaller than the SE, and hence using variance instead of
standard error has caused Distance to report a SE and CV that is smaller than it
should be.

We will issue a new release of Distance shortly.  Since P2 is the default
estimator of encounter rate variance, we recommend that CDS and MCDS point
transect analyses that were run in Distance 6.0 Release 1 and 2 be re-run in
the new release to check the analytic variance estimator.

We apologize for any problems caused by this bug.

--

Hi Buddy,

Yes, I think this will work, if you're willing to assume that the
detection function from the calibration surveys applies to your original
surveys -- this is an assumption you can't test.

How do you do the analysis?  Do would do a standard detection function
modelling analysis of the distances from the calibration survey and use
this to get an estimated P (average probability of detection between
distance 0 and the truncation distance), SE on P and DF on P.  You'd
then enter these into Distance as multipliers.  Lastly, you'd run an
analysis on the original survey where, instead of fitting a detection
function (under detection function you specify a uniform key function
and 0 adjustment terms), you'd use the P, SE(P) and df from the
calibration survey.  This kind of thing is described under "Multipliers"
in the Distance help, although not exactly in this context.

Hope this helps,

  - Len Thomas

 double-sampling (calibration) is the serious option.

Murray makes a good point regarding distance effects on point counts and
models based on temporally replicated visits, and Efford and Dawson's 2009
Auk paper is a useful accomplishment indeed.  Nonetheless, N-mixture and

related MLE models have been and continue to be useful tools for

understanding relationships between relative abundance/density and habitat
and landscape features.  I guess Buddy's decision could be influenced by
whether his goal is solely to estimate population size (perhaps among years

or sites) or to investigate why population size varies.  Regardless, I

certainly wouldn't dismiss entire suites of modeling approaches based on the

conclusions of a single research simulation.

I agree with Len and Murray that resampling for sake of estimating a
detection function is reasonable, especially if you can use the same

observers and qualify that the factors influencing detection haven't changed
much over time.  But my original point is that if you have data based on
temporally repeated visits, then you have a set of rigorous modeling tools

available that might complement your data, without having to invest the
likely significant resources in resampling.  Best,

Matt

Hi Matt, all

I guess the question boils down to what are the assumptions underlying=20
the "rigorous modelling tools" you are referring to.

It is not enough that the modelling tool is rigorous, you also need that=20
the underlying assumptions of a rigorous method hold to a reasonable=20
extent in the practical example at hand.

What the Efford and Dawson's 2009 Auk paper showed is something which is=20
essentially intuitive. If there is a fair amount of unmodeled=20
heterogeneity which is not accounted for in your model, in particular=20
from distance from the transect (which is likely the case in Buddy's=20
study, given his description), then the N-mixture model (and others)=20
might not be ideal and lead to considerable bias. So in the case at=20
hand, it seems like the N-mixture model could indeed lead to=20
considerable bias. So while I agree with you that one should not dismiss=20
entire suites of modeling approaches based on a single study, I think=20
one might want to dismiss said entire suit of modelling approaches under=20
those scenarios where the corresponding assumptions do not hold. That=20
will be valid for any modelling approach.

Note that the assumption that the detection function is the same in the=20
survey and in the calibration study will be however a leap of faith, yet=20
one that people often make. Assessing whether factors that might have=20
changed (like observers, or weather conditions, or helicopter type, say)=20
have a strong influence in the detection function might be a way to test=20
to what extent you might be going wrong if you take the calibration route.

Cheers,

T.

Hi Tiago-

Greetings from the other side of the planet.  I couldn't agree more that
assessing assumptions of models is critical (especially given the
constraints of data already sampled), which is exactly why I highlighted th=
e
primary assumption of mixture models based on temporally replicated visits

mixture model (Dail and Madsen 2011) for when closure is unlikely.

I disagree, however, that assessing assumptions is the sole or even primary
criteria with which to make a decision in this case because understanding
the research goal (which I admittedly do not) is equally as important.  If
the goal is to simply estimate absolute abundance of some population,
without modeling it as a function of ecological variables, then Efford and
Dawson's (2009) simulations suggest that the N-mixture model may not be
ideal.  If the goal, however, is to model relative abundance as a function
of some variables representing, for example, landscape configuration or
habitat structure, then mixture models based on temporally replicated visit=
s
might be suitable.

Best,

Matt

IT CONTAINS VITAL INFORMATION

Welcome to the DISTANCE SAMPLING e-mail discussion list. The purpose of
this list is to promote the sharing of ideas and information among
researchers and practitioners interested in distance sampling techniques
(see below). Suitable topics for postings include:

o Questions about distance sampling survey design and analysis.
o New methodological developments in distance sampling.
o Use of software tools (program DISTANCE and other software).
o News about up-coming meetings, workshops and conferences where
   distance methods will be discussed.
o Jobs in distance sampling fields.

Instructions for subscribing, unsubscribing, posting and getting help
are given in subsequent sections.

Before posting any messages,

** PLEASE READ THE LIST GUIDELINES **

which are given near the end of this file. Very briefly the key points
are:

o Make sure distance-sampling is the appropriate forum for your message.
   If you are unsure ask the list owner first.
o Use informative subject lines.
o If seeking a reply, include your address in the body of your message.
   Offer to compile the replies you recieve and summarize them to
   the list.
o If replying, consider whether to reply to the sender rather than
   the list.
o Send plain text only (no Word or encoded files or other attachments).
o Do not post commercial advertising (however announcements about
   jobs, conferences, non-commercial software, etc are okay).

 ========================================================================
Background
 ========================================================================

Distance sampling is a widely used technique for estimating the abundance
of biological populations. Distance sampling methods include line
transects, point transects (variable circular plots), cue counting,
trapping webs and migration counts. An introduction to the the
methods is given in the following book:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers, D.L,
and Thomas, L. (2001). Introduction to Distance Sampling.  Oxford University
Press, Oxford, UK.

A previous edition of the book is freely available for download on the
internet
at http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

Recent methodological developments and applications are also discussed in
biological journals such as the Journal of Wildlife Management, Ecology,
Biometrics, and the Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Ecological
Statistics.

The standard software for the design and analysis of distance sampling
data is program Distance. Newer versions are fully windows-based with an
intuitive point-and-click interface. The software is freely available for
download from the Distance home page
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I am attempting to analyze distance data on four different species of birds
to obtain density estimates for Iowa.  I have three strata for which I wish
to obtain estimates based on different types and quality of habitat.  I also
have three weather covariates that I wish to include in the model (cloud
cover, wind speed, and air temperature).  A species-specific model including
stratification and no covariates seems to run fine and obtains acceptable
estimates.  However, when I run the same model including a single covariate,
I get the following error:

      ** Warning: Some parameters are very highly correlated. **
** Warning: Parameter  2 is at an upper bound. **
 ** Internal Error 50: Mismatched strata -            1           0  **
 ** Internal Error 50: Mismatched strata -            2           1  **
 ** Internal Error 50: Mismatched strata -            3           2  **
 ** Internal Error 23: ier -            3           0           2
2

I get this error for more than one species and am not sure whether this is
an issue with the data themselves or whether it is a data formatting/input
issue.  Regardless of the error message, however, the density estimates from
the model are still well estimated (CVs are <10 and confidence intervals are
acceptable).  I was wondering if anyone would be able to point me in the
right direction as to where I can obtain information on this error and/or
learn how to fix it?

I hope I have provided enough information to understand the question.  If
not, please let me know.

Thanks in advance,

Tyler Harms
